n: Isaiah 5 opens with a song about a vineyard on a fertile hill. The “beloved” who owns it is God.

f.g: The Lord, as owner of the vineyard.
Hebrew: “a horn, son of oil” — a rich slope.

n: He did everything for his vineyard: fenced it, cleared stones, planted the best vines, built a watchtower and a winepress. But it produced only wild, sour grapes.
God asks the people of Jerusalem and Judah to judge between Him and His vineyard.
What more could He have done? Yet it produced only wild grapes. Compare the Lord’s lament in Zenos’s allegory of the olive tree.

f.w: What could have been done more to my vineyard

n: So He will remove its hedge and wall, letting animals trample and eat it.

f.g: Come now; an expression to get attention.

n: He will leave it unpruned and untilled, overgrown with briers and thorns, and command the clouds to withhold rain.

The meaning: the vineyard is Israel, and Judah is His favored plant. He looked for justice (mishpat) but found bloodshed (mispach); for righteousness (tsedaqah) but heard a cry (tse‘aqah). Isaiah uses a Hebrew wordplay.

f.w: he looked for judgment, and behold, oppression
f.g: A pun in Hebrew: mishpat (justice) vs. mispach (bloodshed).

n: The first of six woes: against land-grabbers who buy up house after house and field after field until they live alone, pushing out the poor.
God warns that many grand houses will be left empty and cities deserted.
Harvests will fail badly: ten acres of vines will produce only about six gallons of wine, and planted seed will return only a tenth of itself.

f.g: A liquid measure of about 6 gallons (22 liters).
A dry measure, about 6 bushels; an ephah is one-tenth of a homer.

n: Woe to those who start drinking early and party into the night.
Their feasts have music and wine, but they give no thought to what the Lord is doing.
So the people go into captivity “because they have no knowledge” — they ignored God. Their nobles starve and the crowds die of thirst.
The grave (Sheol) opens its mouth wide to swallow the proud and partying multitudes.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the grave or world of the dead.

n: Both lowly and mighty will be humbled, and the proud brought low.
But the Lord will be exalted through His just judgment and shown holy through righteousness.
Lambs will graze in the ruins of the rich, and strangers will eat in the deserted estates.
Woe to those who drag their sins behind them like a cart pulled with ropes — tied to their wrongdoing.
They mock God: “Let Him hurry up and do His work so we can see it!” — taunting His warnings.
Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who swap darkness for light and bitter for sweet. Moral confusion is a mark of a decaying society.

f.w: call evil good, and good evil

n: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes.
Woe to those whose only heroism is in drinking and mixing strong drink.
They take bribes to declare the guilty innocent and deny justice to the innocent.
Like stubble in fire, their roots will rot and their blossoms blow away as dust, because they rejected God’s law and word.

f.w: as the fire devoureth the stubble

n: God’s anger strikes His people; hills tremble and bodies lie in the streets. Yet “his hand is stretched out still” — a refrain repeated in Isaiah 9–10. It can describe continuing judgment, and Latter-day Saints also see in it God’s outstretched hand of mercy.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

n: God will raise a banner to distant nations and whistle for them to come quickly. Historically this meant Assyria’s armies; Latter-day Saints also see the latter-day gathering to Christ’s ensign.

f.g: A banner or flag raised as a rallying point.

n: They will come tireless and alert, belts fastened and sandal straps unbroken — ready and unstoppable.

f.g: Belt; tightening it meant being ready for action.

n: Their arrows are sharp and bows strung; horses’ hooves are hard as flint and chariot wheels spin like a whirlwind. Some readers see hints of modern transportation in this imagery.
They roar like young lions, seize their prey, and carry it off with none to rescue it.
Their roar will be like the sea’s; the land will be covered in darkness and sorrow, and the sky’s light will grow dark.
